items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system
items.why: Source of the quotation. The deployer's duty: monitor; where use in line with the instructions may present a risk, inform the provider or distributor and the authority and suspend use; on a serious incident, inform first the provider, then importer or distributor and the authorities. If the provider cannot be reached, Article 73 applies to the deployer. Article 26 is not marked amended. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 73: Reporting of serious incidents
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer, becomes aware of the serious incident
items.why: Source of the figure. The reporting duty is the provider's: immediately once a causal link (or its reasonable likelihood) is established and in any event within 15 days of awareness; two days for a widespread infringement or serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure; 10 days where a person has died. An incomplete first report is allowed. The provider must not alter the system in a way that affects later evaluation before informing the authorities. Article 73 is not marked amended. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 3: Definitions
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to any of the following
items.why: Defines a serious incident by its consequence: death or serious harm to health; serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure; infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights; serious harm to property or the environment. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 113: Entry into force and application
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i) and (ii) (marked AMENDED)
items.quote: 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III
items.why: The date. Chapter III Sections 1 to 3, which include Article 26, apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I products. Article 73 sits in Chapter IX, which falls under the general application date of 2 August 2026, but it bites only on systems classified as high-risk. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Draft guidance, Article 73 AI Act: incident reporting (high-risk AI systems)
items.locator: Section 3.2 'Deployers of high-risk AI Systems', paragraphs (47) and (48), PDF page 10
items.quote: Immediately should be understood as within 24 hours.
items.why: The Commission's reading of the deployer's duty: tell the provider within 24 hours, and treat the provider as unreachable if it does not answer within 24 hours. A consultation draft (closed 7 November 2025) with passages left blank; no final version was found. Its landing page still says the rules apply from August 2026, which predates the 2026 amendments. Not binding.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 33: Notification of a personal data breach
items.quote: The controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts relating to the personal data breach, its effects and the remedial action taken.
items.why: The UK duty that already applies when an AI failure exposes, alters or loses personal data: notify the regulator without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, in phases if need be; a processor must tell the controller; every breach is documented. Article 34, read alongside, requires telling the people affected where the risk to them is high. The text reads 'the Commission' from 30 September 2026.

items.title: Personal data breaches: a guide
items.locator: Opening summary ('At a glance') and section 'What breaches do we need to notify the ICO about?'
items.quote: You must also keep a record of any personal data breaches, regardless of whether you are required to notify.
items.why: The regulator's working guidance on breach reporting: a process to detect, assess, report within the limit and record. Updated 20 August 2025 for the Data (Use and Access) Act. Covers personal data breaches only; an AI system producing unfair or wrong decisions is not in itself a breach.

items.title: The General Product Safety Regulations 2005, regulation 9: Obligations of producers and distributors
items.quote: he shall forthwith notify an enforcement authority in writing of that information
items.why: A UK reporting duty with no fixed number of days: a producer or distributor who knows a consumer product it supplied is unsafe must notify at once, say what action was taken, and co-operate. Relevant only where AI is part of a consumer product. Great Britain version.

items.title: Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 34)
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
items.locator: Abstract, p.1; executive summary, p.9; 'Common reporting framework', p.10; Table 2.2
items.quote: Making only some criteria mandatory streamlines the reporting process.
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary common format for describing an AI incident: 29 criteria, of which seven are mandatory. Useful as a template for an internal incident record. The Commission's draft guidance says the AI Act regime seeks to align with it. The OECD landing page refused automated access; the PDF itself was read.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use
items.why: The governance point in a voluntary framework: mechanisms in place 'and responsibilities are assigned and understood' to supersede, disengage or deactivate a system; incidents and errors communicated to those affected. US framework with no legal force in the UK.

items.title: The Medical Devices (Post-market Surveillance Requirements) (Amendment) (Great Britain) Regulations 2024, regulation 4 (new Part 4A)
items.quote: no later than 15 days after the manufacturer becomes aware of the serious incident
items.why: A UK incident-reporting duty with fixed limits that already covers AI sold as a medical device: the manufacturer reports a serious incident immediately once a causal link is established or reasonably possible and within 15 days of awareness; 2 days for a serious public health threat; 10 days for a death or unanticipated serious deterioration in health. Regulation 44ZG requires preventive or corrective action as soon as possible. Limits: manufacturers of medical devices only; Great Britain; the as-made text (regulation 1 brings it into force six months after making); later amendments not checked.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SUP 15.3: General notification requirements
items.quote: A firm must notify the FCA immediately it becomes aware, or has information which reasonably suggests
items.why: A binding rule for authorised firms that applies whatever the technology: tell the regulator at once of anything that could have a significant adverse impact on its reputation, cause serious detriment to a customer or have serious financial consequences for other firms, including where it may occur in the foreseeable future. An AI system causing customer harm falls within it. Limits: FCA-authorised firms only; not AI-specific. The page shows a last update of 1 June 2026 and a future version dated 18 March 2027.

items.title: The Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018, regulation 11: The duty to notify incidents
items.quote: without undue delay and in any event no later than 72 hours after the operator is aware that a NIS incident has occurred
items.why: The UK reporting clock for operators of essential services (energy, transport, health, water, digital infrastructure): an incident with a significant impact on continuity of the service must be notified to the competent authority within 72 hours. Reaches an AI failure only where it disrupts an essential service. Limits: designated operators only; the page shows no outstanding changes today, but the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would amend this regime and its progress was not checked in this pass.

items.title: In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC: Order Instituting Administrative and Cease-and-Desist Proceedings (Release No. 34-70694)
items.locator: Summary, paragraph 9(D); paragraphs 15 to 21 (events of 1 August 2012)
items.quote: Knight did not have controls and supervisory procedures reasonably designed to guide employees’ responses to significant technological and compliance incidents
items.why: An enforcement decision on the cost of having no rehearsed way to stop an automated system. A faulty deployment sent millions of orders in about 45 minutes; the firm lost over $460 million. The regulator found no written procedures for reviewing deployments or guiding staff through an incident. Limits: United States securities law; automated trading software, not AI; 2013; a settled order, so findings were neither admitted nor denied.

items.title: Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database
items.publisher: arXiv (author's copy; paper for the Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence conference, IAAI-21); author Sean McGregor
items.quote: As a result, companies repeatedly make the same mistakes in the design, development, and deployment of intelligent systems.
items.why: Research case for recording incidents and learning from them, drawing on aviation: without a shared memory of failures the same ones recur. Supports the higher levels of the criterion, where incident reviews change practice. Describes a database then holding more than 1,000 incident reports, compiled largely from press coverage, so it is not a measure of how often incidents occur. Limits: descriptive paper about one database; United States-led; 2020.

items.title: Deployment Corrections: An incident response framework for frontier AI models
items.publisher: arXiv (Institute for AI Policy and Strategy); authors Joe O'Brien, Shaun Ee, Zoe Williams
items.quote: establish or grow dedicated teams to design and maintain processes for deployment corrections, including incident response plans
items.why: Working paper setting out a graded set of responses once a deployed model proves harmful, from restricting users, access or features up to full shutdown, and recommending that the power to apply them is agreed with downstream users in advance. Useful for defining suspension triggers and for what to ask a supplier. Limits: preprint, not peer reviewed; written for developers of the most capable models, not for organisations that use them; a framework, not evidence of effect.

items.title: AI incident reporting: Addressing a gap in the UK’s regulation of AI
items.publisher: The Centre for Long-Term Resilience; author Tommy Shaffer Shane
items.quote: the UK’s regulation of AI currently lacks an effective incident reporting framework
items.why: Independent UK policy report confirming the brief's starting point: there is no general UK regime for reporting AI incidents, only what individual regulators collect. Recommends a reporting system for government's own use of AI first. Limits: a think-tank report, not peer reviewed and not official; its count of over 10,000 incidents comes from news reports; written in June 2024 and addressed to government, not to companies.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: should support End-users and Affected Entities during and following a cyber security incident to contain and mitigate the impacts of an incident
items.why: The UK government code that ties AI incident handling to cyber incident response, as the top level of the criterion asks: an incident management plan and a recovery plan that are created, tested and maintained (6.5), and support for users and affected people during and after an incident, documented and agreed in contracts (10.3). Limits: voluntary; framed around security incidents, not unfair or wrong outputs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested actions GV-1.7-001 (GOVERN 1.7) and MG-2.4-001 to MG-2.4-004 (MANAGE 2.4)
items.quote: Protocols are put in place to ensure GAI systems are able to be deactivated when necessary.
items.why: International comparator, 2024. Turns the suspension question into specific actions for generative AI: protocols so a system can be deactivated, written criteria for when to do so reviewed against risk tolerance, an escalation route to the risk authority, and a plan for telling those affected. A separate document from the 2023 framework already listed. Voluntary; US; no legal force in the UK.
